item.content:encoded:
Glass can be reinforced by a large variety of means, of which I will list four:

  • Glass can be reinforced by thermal tempering. This is the most common type of glass reinforcement.
  • Glass can be made to include a core consisting of a metal mesh. This type is often seen in doors and windows next to doors of industrial buildings.
  • Glass can be reinforced by laminating it together with some type of plastic. This is used in car windshields, and is why they don't break apart into a large number of pieces when shattered.
  • Glass can be reinforced via ion exchange, where the glass is immersed in molten potassium to substitute potassium ions in for some of the sodium ions at the glass surface. This method is commonly used for the glass surface of most modern touch-screen phones.

Well, profanity aside, technology generally requires carrying things. Looking at humans, we have some form of carryall around going all the way back to the earliest known items, and we had "pockets" before we actually had pockets. (Medieval students used the hoods of their robes to carry small books, for example.) Therefore, if we're seeing one unbroken color and we also see technology, it's likely that the one unbroken color is an artificial covering. It's not certain, no — see text — but it's likely.

I see footnote 3 has been incorporated into the text, though.

item.content:encoded:
Alright… Not really much I can say about this. The concept is pretty freakin' awesome, the execution of said concept is okay, but I have a bit of a problem. Namely the containment procedures.

My first major problem with them is the whole thing with the armed guards. This is a Safe class object with no current ability to affect anything within this reality beyond one's perception of it. Said perception change is in itself minor. With that being said, there are far more dangerous objects which the personnel involved could guard with such an action being a better use of their abilities. As it stands, guarding this thing probably consists of standing around for three hours with a weapon in hand, and occasionally checking to make sure someone's authorized to be there.

That last bit of my previous statement leads into my next problem with containment procedures: the level of authorization required.

Constant monitoring of SCP-419 must take place from the viewing bay in order to ensure that the view through SCP-419 does not change significantly. In the event that it does, contact Site Director █████. Access to SCP-419 is prohibited except under special circumstances and permission from Site Director.

First off, those two statements seem to contradict each other(at least from my point of view). Constant monitoring from the viewing bay would seem to imply a certain level of access to the object in the first place. Then there's the fact that the object has to be cleaned regularly. Both of the aforementioned actions in no way imply special circumstances, and are so routine that a Site Director shouldn't be involved with them to the extent implied.

That leads into my final complaint regarding that section of the containment procedures. As stated in the second paragraph, this is a Safe class object which has no effect on this reality beyond one's perceptions of it, with that effect not being in any way harmful to your average person. As long as you're careful and don't break the damn thing, there's not gonna be a problem. As such, there is no legitimate reason for a Site Director to have to approve any and all access to the object. These are busy people, and should not have to approve someone(especially if they have the appropriate clearance level) to access a Safe class SCP. There are people lower on the totem pole who are wholly capable of determining whether or not it's a good idea to let someone do such a thing.

So, yeah. The exceedingly excessive nature of the containment procedures have caused me to downvote this. Should the containment procedures be revised appropriately, I will return to a neutral vote or upvote, depending on the quality of the revision.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
This bothers me. The core aspect of the SCP - that the window shows something not corresponding to the other side, the image of which isn't carried by light - is mentioned once offhandedly and then never given consideration beyond that. Recording devices see nothing, and lenses block the effect, as is demonstrated by glasses and contacts, yet the thermoplastic barrier doesn't inhibit it at all.

That would be the core focus of the Foundation's investigation of this SCP, I think. This is potentially directly stimulating the optic nerve, or somehow directly implanting memories into observers. Instead, it's just used as a handwave to avoid having to elaborate on anything, as would be required if we could view the other side with clarity, and the ramifications of this thing being a possible cognitohazard are totally ignored. The entire thing is just a vehicle to give a bare-bones description of the aftermath of some war we're supposed to care about for some reason that may or may not actually have been a thing - we don't know. It's not logical to assume we're actually seeing real things on the other side, or that there even is an other side, as it's not light coming through.
